newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Violence-torn Albania, Europe's poorest country.
newsitem.headline: Violence-torn Albania, Europe's poorest country.

text.p: Albania, where parliamentary elections on Sunday seek to end months of turmoil, is Europe's poorest country with huge disparaties between cities and a backward countryside.
More than 1,500 people have died since the outbreak of a rebellion in the south by thousands of protesters who had lost their savings in failed investment schemes.

Parliament declared a state of emergency on March 2 and President Sali Berisha, who blamed the violence on former communists, was re-elected unopposed to a second five-year term by parliament a day later.
He later had to agree to early elections and the appointment of a multi-party government led by his Socialist rivals.

A 7,000-member multinational force is in place to maintain a degree of order, though armed gangs still control many parts of the country. Around 500 observers are overseeing the vote under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

POPULATION: 3.4 million, the average age is 25. Moslems make up about 60 percent of the population, Orthodox Christians 20 percent and Roman Catholics about 12 percent. Religious worship was banned and churches shut in 1967; restrictions were lifted in 1990.
AREA: 28,748 sq km (11,101 sq miles). Much of Albania is mountainous. It is bounded by the Adriatic Sea to the west, Macedonia to the east, Yugoslavia to the north and east and Greece to the south.

POLITICS: Albania has a unicameral parliament. Deputies are being elected in 115 constituencies on a first-past-the-post system with 40 seats allocated on a proportional basis. There are 15 more seats than in last year's election. The president is elected by parliament.

MODERN HISTORY: Albania gained independence in 1912 after 450 years of Turkish rule. It became a monarchy in 1928 under King Zog, who fled after fascist Italy occupied Albania in 1939. Later occupied by Nazi Germany, Albania was liberated by communist-led partisans in 1944.
After a year of interim rule, Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha came to power when a communist-dominated parliament was elected in 1945 and a People's Republic proclaimed in 1946.

Hoxha led a harsh regime for 40 years until his death in 1985, drastically isolating Albania under a policy of self-reliance. Ties with Communist superpowers the Soviet Union were ruptured in 1961 and with China in 1978.
Hoxha was succeeded in 1985 by Ramiz Alia, who cautiously opened the country to the outside world. Popular turmoil and student unrest led to the legalisation of opposition parties.

The communist party won Albania's first multi-party elections in March 1991 and changed its name to the Socialist Party. But its authority faded as Albania grappled with the birth pains of a market economy and political pluralism.
Dozens were killed in food riots during the run-up to the second free elections in March 1992.
The Democratic Party won a landslide victory over the ex-communists. Berisha, a former heart surgeon, became Albania's first non-communist president in April 1992.

International observers criticised the conduct of a general election in May 1996 boycotted by most of the opposition parties who accused the Democrats of rigging the vote. Berisha's party won 122 of 140 seats in parliament.
The collapse of five dubious investment schemes triggered protests in January, mainly in the south. Parliament, under Berisha's control, proclaimed a state of emergency on March 2.
Protests spread throughout the country, large numbers of arms were looted from military depots and thousands of Albanians tried to flee to Italy.

Under international pressure, Berisha named a multi-party government responsible for holding Sunday's election. Opposition Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano, pardoned and freed after four years in jail on fraud charges, poses the biggest challenge to Berisha and his Democrats.
ECONOMY: The economy is Europe's poorest and remains largely dependent on small-scale agriculture. Wages average the equivalent of barely $65 a month.

After four months of unrest, the economy is expected to shrink by at least 10 percent this year, while inflation is forecast to top 70 percent. The lek currency is in steep decline and has already lost 80 percent against the dollar this year.
Registered unemployment hovers at around 20 percent.
Industrial recovery remains hampered by a desperate lack of working capital, a shaky banking system and obscure legal structures.
Foreign investment has dropped to zero and a large chunk of the gross domestic product -- estimated at $3.2 billion last year -- is made up by remissions from some 400,000 Albanians living abroad.
At least $1.2 billion was ploughed into five pyramid investment funds before their collapse.
The main industries are chrome and copper mining, agricultural product processing, textiles, oil products and cement.

DEFENCE: Largely in disarray. The International Institute of Strategic Studies put 1995/96 figures at 60,000 men (20,000 conscripts) for the army, the navy with 2,500 (1,000 conscripts) and the air force with 10,000 (1,800 conscripts).
